name: Raloxifene (Evista)
lead: Raloxifene (brand name Evista) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) approved in the US for treating and preventing osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and for reducing the risk of invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis or at high risk [1][2]. It acts as an estrogen agonist in bone and an antagonist in breast and uterine tissue [2][4].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities it is discussed as an off-label oral option for gynecomastia, including puberty-onset gynecomastia, often alongside or after tamoxifen [5][6]. Published evidence for that use consists of small studies, for example a retrospective review in adolescent boys; it is not an approved indication [1][4].

paras: Raloxifene is used for postmenopausal osteoporosis, though it is less preferred than bisphosphonates, and for reducing breast cancer risk in high-risk postmenopausal women [1]. It is not indicated for treating invasive breast cancer or reducing recurrence [2]. It does not relieve hot flashes and may worsen them [4]. An early trial examined its effects on bone mineral density, cholesterol and the uterine lining in postmenopausal women [3].

A small retrospective chart review reported that raloxifene was effective for pubertal gynecomastia in adolescent boys; Wikipedia notes other SERMs also treat gynecomastia [1]. Grokipedia, citing that kind of data, describes a greater than 50 percent reduction in breast tissue volume in most of the treated boys, but this is a small off-label dataset [4]. Looksmax.org posters describe using raloxifene after or alongside tamoxifen for gynecomastia and ask whether it returns after stopping; other posters argue surgery is preferable [5][6].

Common effects are hot flashes, leg cramps, peripheral edema, flu syndrome, joint pain and sweating [2]. The label carries a boxed warning for increased risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism and for increased risk of death from stroke in women with coronary heart disease or elevated risk; it is contraindicated in pregnancy and in people with a history of venous thromboembolism [2]. Unlike tamoxifen it does not increase uterine hyperplasia or endometrial cancer risk [1].

Raloxifene binds estrogen receptors and its agonist or antagonist action depends on recruitment of coactivators and corepressors to target gene promoters in each tissue [2]. Structural work in 1997 described the molecular basis of agonism and antagonism at the estrogen receptor [7]. Oral bioavailability is about 2 percent owing to first-pass metabolism; it is metabolised by glucuronidation and has a half-life of roughly 28 to 33 hours [1].

In the MORE trial of 7,705 postmenopausal women, raloxifene reduced the risk of new vertebral fractures [8] and reduced breast cancer incidence [9]. The STAR trial compared raloxifene with tamoxifen in high-risk postmenopausal women and found similar invasive-breast-cancer prevention with a lower thromboembolism risk [1][10]. Smaller registered trials have tested raloxifene in schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease and endometriosis [11]. No controlled trial in men with gynecomastia was identified; the evidence is the small retrospective review described above [1].

timeline.event: US approval for prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis [1][4].
US approval for osteoporosis treatment; MORE fracture and breast cancer results published [1][8][9].
STAR trial results comparing tamoxifen and raloxifene published [10].
US approval for breast cancer risk reduction; boxed warning on stroke death risk [1].

lore.intro: Raloxifene comes up on looksmax.org mostly as a gynecomastia drug, often compared with tamoxifen and with surgery [5][6].

claims.believers: Users report that nipple and chest swelling has shrunk on raloxifene and discuss using it after tamoxifen [5].
claims.experts: A small retrospective review in adolescent boys reported improvement with raloxifene; it is not an approved use and no controlled male trial was identified [1].

claims.claim: Gyno may come back after stopping
claims.believers: Posters worry that breast tissue could regrow once raloxifene is stopped [5].
claims.experts: No published study in the sources reviewed has followed relapse after stopping in men.

claims.claim: Surgery is preferable to the drug
claims.believers: Some posters say surgery is better than taking raloxifene and cite fears about side effects [6].
claims.experts: The label lists boxed warnings for blood clots and stroke death in postmenopausal women with cardiovascular risk; these data are from women [2].

card.summary: A prescription SERM approved for women's bone and breast risk, used off-label by men for gynecomastia on thin evidence.
card.note: Boxed warning: blood clots and stroke death; approved only for postmenopausal women.

quick.overview:
Raloxifene is a prescription SERM approved for osteoporosis and breast cancer risk reduction in postmenopausal women. Forum users discuss it as an off-label gynecomastia drug.

For that use, evidence is limited to a small retrospective review in adolescent boys.
quick.mechanism: It blocks estrogen action in breast tissue and mimics it in bone, depending on the tissue's receptor environment.
quick.risks: The label has a boxed warning for blood clots and stroke death; common effects include hot flashes, leg cramps and swelling. It is prescription-only and contraindicated in pregnancy.
